common_name: Fair Bianca Rose (Early David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Fair Bianca is a compact early Austin introduction well suited to smaller beds.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1982, Fair Bianca bears small, fully double, pure white rosette-shaped blooms with a strong, sweet myrrh fragrance, held on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub notably smaller than many later English roses. Its neat habit fits foundation beds and mixed borders where space is limited, and it reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall with reasonable reliability. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and maintain good air circulation, since like many early Austin introductions it can be more prone to black spot than newer, disease-bred cultivars.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Wife of Bath Rose (Early Fragrant Pink David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Wife of Bath, one of David Austin's earliest introductions, stays compact and fits smaller garden spaces.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1969, Wife of Bath is one of his earliest English roses, bearing small, cupped, warm pink double blooms with a strong, sweet myrrh-and-clove fragrance that was influential in establishing the fragrance character later Austin roses became known for. Its compact, bushy habit and reliable rebloom from late spring through fall have kept it in cultivation for decades despite the arrival of many newer, more disease-resistant Austin introductions. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter, and provide good air circulation, since older Austin cultivars can show more susceptibility to black spot than modern disease-bred roses.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Chianti Rose (Early Dark Crimson-Purple David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Chianti is one of David Austin's very first English rose introductions and blooms mainly in a single strong spring flush like its old-garden-rose gallica parentage.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1965, Chianti was one of the earliest roses in the English rose line, bearing large, fully double, deep wine-crimson to purple blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance that reflects its close gallica heritage. Unlike most later, repeat-blooming Austin introductions, Chianti flowers mainly in one heavy, dramatic spring flush with only occasional repeat later in the season, in keeping with its old-garden-rose parentage. Its large, vigorous, arching shrub works well as a specimen or informal hedge. Prune lightly right after the main spring bloom, and provide good air circulation, since this early introduction can be more prone to black spot than newer, disease-bred Austin cultivars.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Crown Princess Margareta Rose (Apricot-Orange Climbing English Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and a sturdy support if trained as a climber; Crown Princess Margareta can be grown as a large shrub or as a short climber on a fence, pillar, or arbor.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training as a climber. Introduced by David Austin in 1999 and named for the Swedish crown princess, this rose bears large, deeply cupped, rosette-shaped blooms in warm apricot-orange with a strong, fruity tea-rose fragrance, opening on long, arching canes that make it equally suited to a large shrub border or a short climbing role. It reblooms in strong flushes from late spring through fall and shows good disease resistance for an Austin rose of its generation. Prune to control size and shape in late winter — lightly if grown as a shrub, or by thinning old wood if trained as a climber — and provide good air circulation to keep foliage clean through the growing season.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Charlotte Rose (Soft Yellow David Austin English Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Charlotte is a mid-1990s Austin introduction bred for improved disease resistance over earlier English rose introductions.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1994, Charlotte bears soft butter-yellow, fully double, rosette-shaped blooms with a light tea-rose fragrance, opening on an upright, well-branched shrub with better disease resistance than many earlier English rose introductions. It reblooms reliably in flushes from late spring through fall, and its clear, gentle yellow color works well paired with pinks, whites, and blues in a mixed border. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain the repeat-flowering cycle.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive
